tagline.text: The High Peak, the Zambales Mountains' highest point, and an 18 km old mining-road trek

location.label: Location
location.text: Palauig, Zambales; the trailhead is Sitio Dampay in Barangay Dampay-Salaza

duration.label: Time needed
duration.text: 2 days and 1 night (a day hike takes strength and experience)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱1,500–3,500 (per person, estimated including transport, registration, guide and meals)

airport.label: Nearest airport
airport.text: Clark International Airport (CRK) or Ninoy Aquino International Airport (MNL)

children.text: Mount Tapulao, about 2,037–2,044 m, is the highest peak in the Zambales Mountains and is also called the High Peak. You climb about 18 km of old mining road from the trailhead to the summit, passing through grassland, forest, pine forest and mossy forest in turn.

Mount Tapulao is a mountain in Palauig, Zambales. At about 2,037–2,044 m (figures vary between sources), it is the highest point in the Zambales Mountains and in the province of Zambales. It is commonly called the "High Peak" and is described as the highest mountain in central Luzon. The name is said to come from the many Sumatran pines that grow here, which are called "tapolaw" in Zambal. Large-scale chromite mining once took place here, and traces of the mine near the summit and structures along the trail remain today. The mining road is now the hiking trail.

What makes the mountain so appealing is how much the vegetation changes over a single climb. The lower slopes are grassland and scrub covered in talahib (a tall grass), the middle slopes are secondary to near-primary broadleaf forest, above roughly 1,800 m there is pine forest, and near the summit there is mossy cloud forest. The forest line is given as around 1,875 m. In clear weather the summit opens up a 360-degree view that is said to take in the Zambales Mountains, Lingayen Gulf to the north, the South China Sea to the west, and as far south as Pundaquit in San Antonio.

The standard route for ordinary hikers starts from the trailhead at Dampay village on the Palauig side. The village is a resettlement site for people who lost their homes in the 1991 Mount Pinatubo eruption, and they are known to act as self-appointed guardians of the mountain. The DENR Region 3 office signed an agreement to protect and develop about 5,000 hectares of the mountain, and the Sangguniang Bayan of Iba declared its part of the mountain an ecotourism destination and protected area. For this reason a guide and registration are required, and you must follow the guidance of the local tourism office.

The climb itself is not easy. It is about 18 km from the trailhead to the summit, about 36 km round trip, mostly on an old mining road strewn with rough rock. The slope is steady, but with little shade and a monotonous track it is a mentally tiring route. One guide gave 6–12 hours to the summit (usually 7–9 hours up and 4–5 hours down). Strong hikers can do it in a day, but most people recommend a 2-day, 1-night trip that stays at a camp partway up and climbs to the summit before dawn. This guide is for travelers with hiking experience. Check the current opening status with the Palauig tourism office first. For preparation, remember three things. First, the trail is almost a straight stone road that is hard on ankles and knees, so bring boots and trekking poles. Second, the water sources are fixed, so plan your water section by section. Third, phone signal is weak, and if you do not come down at the agreed time the guide and village will come looking for you, so tell the registration office your schedule accurately. Budgets vary a lot between guides, from about ₱1,500 to ₱3,500 per person, depending on transport and how the guide fee is split.

blocks.title: Highest peak of the Zambales Mountains

children.text: From the summit you take in the ridgelines of the Zambales Mountains, Lingayen Gulf and the western sea at a glance. Early morning on a clear day is sharpest. Cloud closes the view, so if you want a summit sunrise, the usual approach is to leave the mid-mountain camp before dawn.

The road once used to haul chromite is now the hiking trail. It is wide and easy to follow, but stony, hard on the soles of your feet, and shady only in places. Many guides refer to points along the trail by kilometer, which makes it easy to gauge your progress.

Sumatran pine forest begins at roughly 1,800 m, and near the summit you reach mossy cloud forest. Unlike the grassland below, the temperature drops sharply and fog forms easily, so the atmosphere changes completely. A campsite is said to lie in the pine forest.
Mining pits near the summit and traces of structures along the trail remain. It is interesting to see the mountain's history and industrial heritage, but do not go close to old structures.

blocks.title: Dampay village and the Bagsit River

children.text: The trailhead village of Dampay is a settlement for people displaced by Pinatubo. A trail below the village is said to lead on to the starting point for whitewater rafting on the Bagsit River. Before and after your hike, respect the village's circumstances and ask local guides for help.
The most common plan is to sleep at the mid-mountain camp (the "Bunker," about 16 km along) and climb to the summit before dawn. At night the temperature can drop to about
or lower, so you need warm gear.

There is also a multi-day traverse that starts from Barangay Labney in Mayantoc (Tarlac) and comes down to Palauig. It is said to be longer and more varied, and a guide is practically essential. For first-timers we recommend the Palauig route.

items.title: Standard 2 days and 1 night route
items.subtitle: Start at Dampay village, camp at the Bunker, summit before dawn

children.text: Register at the Dampay village registration office, meet your guide, and set out from the trailhead.
Fill up with water at the water point about 10 km along and have a snack.
Reach the Bunker camp about 16 km along, pitch tents and cook dinner.
The next morning, switch on your headlamp and set out for the summit.
Enjoy the sunrise and views from the summit and take photos.
Return to the camp, pack up and descend to the trailhead.
Times for each section vary greatly with your pace. Start early so you do not come down late.

items.title: Day hike
items.subtitle: For those with the strength and experience

children.text: One guide recommends leaving the trailhead by 3–4 AM at the latest.
Climb without stopping, aiming to reach the summit.
Enjoy the view from the summit and have lunch.
Finish the descent before dark.
A day hike is about 36 km round trip and very tiring. For safety we recommend 2 days and 1 night.

items.title: From Manila to the Palauig trailhead

children.text: Take a Victory Liner bus to Iba or Santa Cruz. It leaves from Cubao or Monumento, takes about 5–6 hours, and the fare is given as about ₱380–420.
Get off at the Dampay-Salaza junction on the highway and take a tricycle about 8 km over a rough road to the trailhead. From Iba by tricycle it takes about
45 minutes–1 hour
A tricycle is given as about ₱450 for a special trip per vehicle, or ₱90–150 per person if shared.
Fares change from year to year. Confirm exact amounts on site.
About 4 hours via NLEX and SCTEX is given.
The last 8 km is a rough road, so a passenger car may be risky. Check whether there is parking near Dampay village.

items.title: From the village to the trailhead

children.text: A tricycle may go as far as the 6 km point, but not every driver will do it.
Find a guide at the registration office and agree on a start time.

Tapulao is most pleasant from November to February. That is when it is coolest and clearest, which makes the grassland sections easier to walk. One guide advises avoiding July–October (typhoon season) and explains that the lower grassland is very hot from March to May.
Night temperatures on the mountain can fall to around 10 degrees or lower, so you need heavy clothing even in the dry season. In the rainy season, leeches (limatik) are said to appear near streams.

blocks.label: Season at a glance
rows: The most recommended time. Nights are cold, so bring warm gear.
The lower grassland is very hot and water can be short.
Not recommended because of leeches, slippery trails and landslide risk.

On the mountain you normally sleep in tents at the mid-mountain camp (the Bunker). There are no restaurants or shops, so you must bring all your food and cooking gear. Water can be refilled at about the 5 km and 10 km points, and the water at the Bunker may dry up in the dry season.

There is lodging in Iba and Palauig town below the mountain. Places to stay overnight in Dampay village are limited, so look into it in advance. It is also common to stay in Iba the night before and travel up in the morning for an early start.

Using a guide run by Dampay village residents and eating local meals is also a good approach. There is not much food to buy in the village, so it is usual to buy rice, instant noodles, canned food, coffee, snacks and a gas burner in Manila or Iba beforehand. Carry out all the trash you generate, and mind noise and photography etiquette in residents' living areas. After the descent, a meal in Iba town fits nicely before your bus to Manila. The last bus times differ by season, so check in advance.
Register at the Dampay-Salaza barangay registration office, and a guide is required. Contact the Palauig tourism office at least 3 days before departure to check whether the mountain is open.
For a day hike you must start by 3–4 AM. Come down before dark.
Refill water at about the 5 km and 10 km points. Water at the Bunker dries up in the dry season, so carry plenty.
Night temperatures can be 10 degrees or lower, so bring warm clothing and a sleeping bag.
The trail is stony and hard on the feet. You need sturdy-soled boots, trekking poles and spare socks.
There is little shade, so wear a hat, sunscreen and long sleeves.
Phone signal is weak or absent, so download offline maps and decide on emergency contacts.
In the rainy season, prepare socks, salt and spray against leeches near streams.

Tapulao is a mountain that requires a guide and advance registration. Entry can be closed by weather or security conditions, so check the latest situation with the Palauig tourism office before you leave.
Do not climb in typhoon season (July–October). Heavy rain makes the trail slippery and brings landslide risk.
A day hike is about 36 km round trip and carries a risk of exhaustion and hypothermia. If you are not feeling well, turn back partway.
Long stretches have almost no shade, so watch out for heatstroke. You will use a lot of water.
Mine pits and old structures are dangerous, so do not go close to them.
The trail has reportedly been closed before for rehabilitation, so always confirm fees and opening rules on site for the latest.
The volcano whose 1991 eruption displaced the people who settled Dampay village, located in nearby Tarlac and Zambales.

blocks.title: Pundaquit and the San Antonio coast

children.text: The coast the summit view reaches to the south, where boat tours to Anawangin and Nagsasa coves depart.
If you want to relax on a beach after the hike, the quiet coves of San Antonio are next along the coast.
A lighthouse island about
10 minutes
by boat from Pundaquit.
